to consumers; capped at 2,500 SF Marijuana Delivery Operator: authorizes the permit holder to take possession from retail stores and microbusinesses and deliver them only in person to consumers Marijuana Transporter: authorizes the permit holder to take possession from cultivation facilities, processing facilities, retail stores, microbusinesses, and other transporters; no direct interaction with consumers. 9 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC License Caps Tier V Cultivation Licenses: Capped at 5 before January 1, 2028 Microbusiness Licenses: 100 reserved for industrial hemp processors/growers, qualifying impact licensees, and USDAqualified farmers before May 1, 2027 At least 55 additional Licenses must be issued by July 1, 2027 Cultivation/Processing licenses for industrial hemp growers or processors: Capped at 20, with no more than 10 cultivation licenses and no more than 10 processing, by May 1, 2027 10 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Part II: What Localities Cannot Do 11 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Virginia Code § 4.1-629(A): State Preemption “No county, city or town shall, except as provided in §4.1-630, adopt any ordinance or resolution that regulates or prohibits the cultivation, processing, possession, sale, distribution, handling, transportation, consumption, use, advertising, or dispensing of marijuana or marijuana products.” 12 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Localities may NOT: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Ban or “opt out” of the cannabis marketplace Impose moratoriums on cannabis business operations Regulate advertising of cannabis or cannabis products Regulate possession limits, product types, potency, or packaging Cap the number of licenses within their boundaries Increase the VCCA Board’s minimum distance/buffer requirements Impose any tax other than the 13.5% local tax 13 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Part III: What Localities Must Do 14 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Local Cannabis Tax Decisions [§ 4.1-1004(B)(1)] • Local cannabis tax rate may not be less than 1% and may not be more than 3.5% • The effective date of any such ordinance is the first day of the second month following the ordinance enactment • Once set, the rate must stay in place for three years 15 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Deadline for Locality Action: No fixed statutory deadline, but must be in place prior to the start of retail cannabis sales on July 1, 2027 Tax Revenue Tax Rate $1M in Retail Sales 1% $10,000 2% $20,000 3.5% $35,000 16 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Local Cannabis Tax Actions 1 2 3 4 Notify the VCCA within 30 days (§ 4.11004(B)(1)) Notify retail cannabis stores and microbusinesses in the locality within 30 days (§ 4.1-1004(B)(1)) Publish notice of the proposed tax (§ 58.13007) Hold a public hearing before enacting/increasing the local tax (§ 58.13007) 17 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Local Cannabis Tax for Towns Note: County tax rates do NOT apply within the limits of any town located therein Towns must independently levy their own local cannabis tax Towns that fail to act will have no local tax revenue from cannabis sales occurring within the corporate limits 18 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Adopt Internal Administrative Procedures [§§ 4.1-1000(G), 4.1-810] Localities will receive communications from the VCCA related to preliminary approvals of licenses by the VCCA in their locality Localities should adopt procedures for receiving and responding to such communications Failure to file a formal objection to any such notification within 30 days automatically waives the locality’s objection to the approval Recommend designation of locality staff for monitoring of CCA communications and drafting a form objection letter for future use Deadline for Locality Action: none, but the sooner the better 19 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Part IV: What Localities May Do 20 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Review Code Conflicts [§ 4.1-629(D) Localities should review their local ordinances to confirm there are no conflicts or inconsistencies with the new state law governing cannabis Identify conflicting local provisions that need repeal or amendment to comply with the new state law Deadline for Locality Action: Start this process with staff; referral to the Planning Commission 21 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Zoning, Land Use, & Business Licenses [§ 4.1-629(C)] Localities retain substantial authority regarding zoning, land use, and business-license requirements, subject to the limitations and preemption provisions of the VCCA. Localities should review and update their local zoning ordinances to provide regulation of cannabis businesses Zoning and land use regulation represent a significant tool for localities to regulate cannabis-related uses in their borders VCCA may deny final licenses if the establishment violates zoning (§ 4.1-1000(H)(3)) 22 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Local Zoning Tools/Options Designating zoning districts for specific cannabis-related uses Requiring conditional use permits or special exceptions – with potential risk Site plan requirements Setback and buffer distances – which may be decreased but not increased from VCCA Board minimums, which are TBD Deadline for Locality Action: Should be in place by May 1, 2027, or sooner 23 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Public Consumption Ordinances Permitted § 4.1-629(B)(1) LOCALITIES MAY ADOPT ORDINANCES PROHIBITING THE ACTS DESCRIBED IN § 4.1-1108 (PUBLIC CONSUMPTION) AND § 4.1-1109 (POSSESSION/CONSUMPTION ON PUBLIC SCHOOL GROUNDS) IN LOCAL PUBLIC PARKS, PLAYGROUNDS, STREETS, OR SIDEWALKS ADJACENT TO ANY PUBLIC STREET LOCAL ORDINANCE MAY PRESCRIBE PENALTY FOR VIOLATIONS, BUT PROVIDES NO MAXIMUM OR MINIMUM PENALTY Deadline for Locality Action: Q4 2026 to Q1 2027 24 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Buffer Reductions Allowed [§ 4.1-629(B)(2)] • Authorizes localities to adopt ordinances decreasing the VCCA Boardpromulgated minimum distance requirements: • Between Retail Marijuana Stores and Microbusinesses; or • Between a Retail Marijuana Store/Microbusiness and any hospital, public, private or parochial school or institution of higher learning, or child day program 25 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Buffer Distances, con’t Localities may only decrease buffers; they cannot impose stricter distance requirements than those set by the VCCA Board Localities should consider running a GIS suitability analysis (reviewing location of schools, day cares, parks, etc.) before adopting or stacking buffers Overlapping setbacks can unintentionally eliminate all feasible sites in the locality Deadline for Locality Action: Q4 2026 to Q1 2027 26 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Establish Hours of Sale [§ 4.1-630] 01 02 03 Authorizes cities, towns, and counties of unincorporated areas to adopt ordinances fixing the hours during which cannabis may be sold in the locality Provides any such ordinance shall provide for fine and penalties enforced as a Class 1 misdemeanor, with the right of appeal under § 16.1-106 Once passed, the clerk of the governing body must certify the ordinance and transmit it to the VCCA Board Deadline for Locality Action: Q4 2026 to Q1 2027 27 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Regulate Hemp/Tobacco Retail Locations [§ 15.2-912.4] Authorizes localities to adopt ordinances regulating the retail sale locations of retail tobacco products or hemp products intended for smoking Localities may prohibit a retail sale location on property within 1,000 linear feet of a child day center or public, private, or parochial schools Deadline for Locality Action: Q4 2026 to Q1 2027 28 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Part V: Risk Areas 29 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC De Facto Bans Overly restrictive zoning, buffers, or use-permit denials may be challenged as a de facto ban inconsistent with the statewide marketplace The most defensible ordinances generally: • Identify districts where cannabis uses are permitted • Maintain objective approval criteria • Use traditional zoning standards • Create a record demonstrating reasonable accommodation or licensed cannabis businesses 30 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC By Right vs. SUP and the De Facto Ban Issue • Requiring a special or conditional use permit carries its own preemption risk under § 4.1-629(A) and CAN BECOME A DE FACTO BAN if denials rest on generalized opposition rather than objective planning and safety findings • Objective site development requirements (lighting, screening, security, parking, etc.) generally present lower preemption risk than subjective use-permit denials 31 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC License Objection Process [§ 4.1-810] Upon preliminary license approval, VCCA notifies locality; locality has 30 days to object Objections might include: Failure to object waive local challenge 32 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC •Zoning noncompliance •Land Use violations •Local Ordinance conflicts •Factual errors Litigation Risks De Facto Bans: The locality does not expressly prohibit cannabis use, but it leaves no realistic path to operate within the locality Arbitrary and Capricious Denials: Denials based on generalized concerns about cannabis, or public opposition, rather than objective land use impacts Equal Treatment Claims: Cannabis businesses treated differently than comparable commercial uses without reasonable land use justification 33 | ©2026 Objective Site Standards Operational Conditions Repeated Permit Denials Administrative Procedures 34 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC Regs That Effectively Prohibit Licensing Part VI: Departmental Checklists taxes from cannabis businesses Update business license application forms and review procedures for cannabis-specific operations Coordinate with VCCA on tax-rate notices and collection processes 36 | Impaired driving detection and enforcement protocols • Security and crime prevention planning for cash-heavy licensed retail businesses • Evidence handling and chain of custody procedures • Coordination with the VCCA on enforcement investigations • Training and policy updates reflecting the changes to the Virginia law This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 37 | ©2026 local retailers within 30 days of the local tax ordinance enactment (§ 4.1-1004) • Track incoming correspondence from the VCCA • Calendar the 30-day objection deadlines for all license applications provided preliminary approval by the VCCA (§ 4.11000(G)) • Designate recipient; create routing protocol; establish legal review timeline; create objection template 38 | ©2026 Sands Anderson PC title: Notice of Special Called Meeting of the Planning Commission to discuss proposed revisions to the Comprehensive Plan and Zoning Ordinance related to solar facilities.
text: COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT botetourtva.gov 57 S. Center Drive Daleville, VA 24083 P: (540) 928-2080 F: (540) 473-2018 NOTICE BOTETOURT COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION The Botetourt County Planning Commission will hold a work session on Monday, December 07, 2026, at 4:00 PM at 57 S. Center Drive, Daleville VA 24083 to discuss proposed revisions to the Comprehensive Plan and the Zoning Ordinance related to solar facilities. While no public hearing or comment period will be held during the work session, the public is welcome to attend. The regular session will follow at 6:00 PM. During the regular 6:00pm session, a public hearing will be held on the following items: Blue Ridge District: Botetourt County Board of Supervisors requests a Rezoning from the Agricultural (A1) Use District to the Business (B-1) Use District with possible proffered conditions as well as a Special Exception Permit for “smaller minimum district sizes in accordance with section 25-224”. The purpose of this project is to expand the existing parking lot and to add outdoor seating for the Blue Ridge branch library. This property totals 2.17 acres, is located at 28 Avery Row, and is identified on Tax Maps as parcel 112-4C. Fincastle District: Calderon Montalvan and Claudia E. Martinez Aguirre request a Special Exception Permit for a Special Events Facility in the Agricultural (A-1) Use District, with possible conditions, in accordance with Sec. 25-73. The primary purpose of this request is to bring the existing library facility into full zoning compliance with the County Code and to accommodate necessary site improvements. The A-1 use district permits a maximum of 15% impervious surface coverage. The property's existing coverage of approximately 32% already exceeds this threshold, making it nonconforming with the current ordinance. In addition to this non-conformity, the library use itself is not a permitted use within the A-1 use district. A public library is, however, listed as a permitted use under the B-1 use district. Rezoning to B-1 would resolve both nonconformities: the district's 60% maximum impervious surface allowance comfortably accommodates the existing coverage, and the use itself would become fully compliant. The proposed rezoning would also support several site improvements. The existing storage shed would be relocated from the north side of the property to the east side, eliminating a current setback non-conformity while creating space for additional parking. The project would add approximately ten (10) new parking spaces to meet growing visitor demand, along with a new concrete pad to provide expanded outdoor seating for patrons. These improvements would increase impervious surface coverage from approximately 32% to 34.5% - a modest increase that remains well within the 60% maximum allowed under B-1 zoning. Reclassifying the parcel to B-1 will resolve the property's existing non-conformities and allow the library to continue serving, and improve access for, the citizens of Botetourt County. The request applies to a 21.459-acre parcel (Tax Map Section 101, Parcel 38), adjacent to Roanoke Road (US Route 220) and College Drive (SR Route 656) containing the "Wellington Multi-Family Community" development. Page 16 of 26 Page 17 of 26 Page 18 of 26 SEP NARRATIVE On behalf of WEBT Holdings, LLC (Owner/Applicant), we are providing the narrative below as supplemental information to support the attached application for a Special Exception Permit (SEP). This request will apply to Tax Parcel 101-38, consisting of 21.459 acres, to allow for additional density for proposed multi-family dwellings on the property. Project Narrative WEBT Holdings, LLC is the Owner of the subject property. The property currently contains a mix of zoning districts including A-1 (Agricultural District), R-2 (Low-Medium Density Residential District), R-3 (Medium Density Residential District), and B-1 (Business District). This property is also located within the Gateway Crossing Overlay District and the Community Business Subdistrict, which essentially overrides the base zoning districts due to additional specific development standards. This request is for a Special Exception Permit to allow for increased density for multi-family development within this Overlay District. The maximum allowable by-right density is 8 units per acre. The Overlay District allows the maximum density to be increased to 26 units per acre with a Special Exception Permit. The proposed maximum density for this SEP request is 14.5 units per acre. Existing Conditions The property fronts on Roanoke Road, Route 220, to the east, and College Drive, Route 658, to the north. There is an existing cemetery located to the south. The remaining adjacent property to the south and west is zoned Agricultural. There is an existing creek crossing the property near the western boundary, which is not within the portion of the property that is being developed. This project is currently under construction. The approved plans include construction of 2 mixed-use buildings located along Route 220 on the eastern portion of the property, as well as 4 multi-family buildings and a pool building further back from Route 220. The plans also include other necessary improvements to support the proposed buildings, such as parking and utility extensions. Planned Improvements The proposed improvements are shown on the previously approved construction plans for “Wellington Multi-Family Community” and will remain largely unchanged as a result of this request. The 2 proposed buildings located at the front of the property are proposed to be revised from mixed-use buildings to multi-family buildings only. The commercial space originally planned for the 1st floor will be revised to additional multi-family space. This will consist of 18 additional multi-family units on the 1st floor of Building 1. The 1st floor of Building 2 will be revised to consist of 10 additional multi-family units as well as amenity/common areas for all residents of the community to use. These common areas (noted as Clubhouse area on the Architectural plans) are expected to include Fitness Center, Mail Room, Recreation Area, and Kitchen and Sitting Areas, as well as Office Space that will be used for management of the property. Preliminary architectural floor plans are included for Buildings 1 and 2 as part of this SEP application (Exhibits B, C, and D). Re-imagining these 1st floor spaces for multi-family uses rather than commercial space will allow for the Wellington Multi-Family Community to be more consistent and cohesive throughout the development and will preserve a much more tight-knit residential feel within the community. The removal of the commercial space will also have significant advantages to the Site Design for this project. Required parking on the site is reduced by approximately 100 spaces, which allows for a significant increase in landscape areas on the site. The updated parking is primarily located on the southern side of the site which allows for the development to provide additional separation from the southern property line closest to the cemetery. The large retaining wall that was planned for this area will be significantly reduced or eliminated completely. Page 19 of 26 An updated Zoning Plan is included with the application as EX-A, dated September 30, 2026, showing the updated and reduced parking areas. The by-right maximum density of multi-family units in this part of the Overlay District is 8 units/acre. It should be noted that multi-family units located within mixed-use buildings do not count toward this maximum density. Therefore, under the currently approved plan, the units on the upper floors of Buildings 1 and 2 did not count toward this density requirement. Removal of the commercial spaces will result in all units now counting toward the maximum density, which results in the need for this SEP request to increase the maximum density to 14.5 units/acre. It is important to note that only 28 additional units are being added to the project as a part of this revision. The currently approved plan includes 276 apartment units as well as +/-39,000 s.f. of commercial space. The proposed plan replaces the commercial space with 28 additional units for a total of 304 apartment units on the property. Stormwater Management The approved development includes two stormwater management facilities to serve the project. There is an above-ground detention facility located at the southwest corner of the development and an underground detention facility located at the northeast corner of the development. The current request will result in a decrease in the overall development footprint and impervious area due to the decrease in required parking and, therefore, will reduce overall stormwater impacts. Access and Traffic A new right-in, right-out entrance from Route 220 has been approved by VDOT as part of the site plan review process for this development. This entrance will include new right turn lane improvements and will have adequate sight distance and spacing from other existing entrances and crossovers. The current request will result in an overall decrease in the amount of traffic generated by the development, which will be a benefit to the Route 220 corridor and the surrounding road network. This decrease is created by the elimination of the commercial space within Buildings 1 and 2. Public Facilities This development will be served by public water and sewer. The approved plans include extension of public water and sewer mains into the property to serve the new buildings. The proposed water and sewer extensions will remain unchanged as a result of this request. However, it should be noted that the proposed residential units are anticipated to result in less water and sewer demand than the currently approved commercial space. The request is anticipated to have little or no impact to other public services, including schools, parks/recreation, and fire/rescue. Comprehensive Plan and Gateway Crossing Area Plan This property is designated for Mixed Use Neighborhood Commercial development on the Botetourt County Future Land Use Map in the Envision 2045 Comprehensive Plan. The Mixed Use Neighborhood Commercial future land use specifies “a range of commercial uses” and indicates that “associated residential development should include higher density housing types such as apartments or townhouses.” The proposed SEP request and multi-family use is consistent with the Mixed Use Neighborhood Commercial designation, particularly when taken in context with the surrounding Mixed Use Neighborhood Commercial land. There is already a significant amount of existing commercial development along this section of the Route 220 corridor, including directly to the north, to the south, and on the opposite side of Route 220 from this project. The proposed multi-family project is in a central location to complement and support these existing commercial establishments. Page 20 of 26 This project also furthers the goals of the Comprehensive Plan in other ways. The development is providing pedestrian accommodations throughout the development and across the frontage of the property, which is a characteristic of the Mixed Use Neighborhood Commercial land use. In addition to this, the project has a “walkable and compact character” and contributes to the “mix of densities and intensity of uses” within the larger overall context of the area. In addition to its consistency with the Future Land Use Map, the proposed SEP request is also in conformance with many of the Goals, Objectives, and Policies outlined in Botetourt County’s Envision 2045 Comprehensive Plan, some of which are outlined below. Development Goals: • “Reduce or restrict multiple access points off major travel routes to preserve capacity of road networks.” • “Construct pedestrian accommodations along U.S. Route 220 to connect existing residential and commercial uses.” The proposed request condenses access to one entrance, which furthers the Development Goals of the Comprehensive Plan and is consistent with VDOT Access Management initiatives. The proposed entrance is centrally located to maximize separation from existing entrances and crossovers. Goal/Objective: • “Secure and preserve woodlands, waterways, and natural assets to ensure easy access to outdoor recreation and the high quality of life synonymous with Botetourt County. In the same breath, we strive to balance preservation with necessary growth to create communities that are integrated into the natural environment, not separate.” The project concentrates the development towards the front of the property near Route 220 and preserves the area in and around the existing creek located at the rear of the site. The developed area is compact and utilizes the available property efficiently. Summary The proposed request is consistent with the Future Land Use Maps in the Botetourt County Comprehensive Plan. This project will allow for the development of much-needed housing along an important and growing corridor. The project will allow this property to be enhanced with new buildings, parking areas, landscaping improvements, and a vibrant residential community that will complement the surrounding commercial corridor. The proposed development will also provide additional housing options in an important area of the County, which is of utmost importance due to the current shortage of housing in our region. As outlined in this narrative and supporting documentation, the proposed request represents a minor change from the existing plan that is already approved and under construction. This SEP will reduce impacts to the overall transportation network, existing public utilities, and other services. The proposed SEP request will allow this property to be developed as a consistent and cohesive new community that will provide an attractive residential option for current and future residents of Botetourt County. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Project Description The applicant requests Pattern Book approval for the residential portion of a mixed-use development consisting of ten for-rent, triplex townhome dwellings. The Depot at Fighting Creek is located south of Anderson Highway along Old Buckingham Road west of Mann Road. The property is zoned VC-PD and is designated Gateway Business in the County’s Future Land Use Plan. Figure 1: Site Location Project Location The residential buildings will be oriented with their primary entrances and front façades facing internal streets. Each residential building is proposed to contain two 1,323-square-foot units and one 1,376square-foot unit, for a total of 4,022 square feet per building. The middle unit will have three bedrooms and the two side units will have two bedrooms. This request is associated with the approved rezoning case 21-01-REZ (Ordinance O-2021-04). Proffered Condition #2, Project Layout and Building Design, states: Figure 2: Site Layout “The project layout (general location of buildings, uses, and open space) and the exterior facades of buildings (architectural design and materials) within the development shall generally reflect the following exhibits.” The referenced exhibits include Exhibit #3 – “Residential Units,” dated January 7, 2021, which establishes the intended architectural character and design of the residential buildings within the development. (See Figure 3). Staff initially recommended approval of the Pattern Book application at the October 6, 2026, Planning Commission meeting, but suggested deferral after questions arose regarding whether the initial submittal “generally” reflected the proffered conditions. Concerns were identified regarding whether the proposed designs adequately reflected the intent of Proffered Condition #2 and the referenced residential exhibit. The Planning Commission voted to defer the application until the November 4, 2026, meeting. The application was subsequently deferred to the December 1, 2026, meeting to allow for revisions to the Pattern Book and further consideration of the proposed residential designs. 2|Page 14 Figure 3: Elevations proffered with 21-01-REZ Figure 4: Proposed Elevations Following the deferral, staff provided the applicant with suggested modifications to the residential elevations to better align the submittal with the original proffers. Revisions to the elevations include adding side projections to Plan A with additional windows, reversing the porch roof orientation on Plan A, and adding roof brackets. However, the applicant declined to make some of staff’s requested modifications and can speak to these items during the meeting. These include providing a more recessed middle unit along the front and rear elevations, providing enhanced siding materials, and incorporating a more detailed architectural feature within the gable. Separate from the residential units, the three proposed commercial buildings will be reviewed individually through the Pattern Book approval process at the time of building permit application. ALTAVISTA COMBINED SCHOOL CONSTRUCTION CONTRACT AWARD The Board of Supervisors at their July meeting approved using the Construction Management method to renovate the Altavista Combined School using RRMM as the architectural firm to lead the design effort. Next, the County issued a Request for Qualifications for firms that would be interested in managing the project. Nine (9) construction firms responded, and the School Board narrowed the list to five (5) offerors to proceed to the proposal stage. Four (4) proposals were received, and these firms were interviewed on November 4th by the School Board, with the Board of Supervisors joint committee members participating in the interviews. After the interviews, English Construction Company, Inc. was the highest scorer and recommended to manage the project. Negotiations with English have included input from RRMM, School Administration, the County Attorney, and County staff, resulting in the attached contract. This is a standard AIA A133 contract modified with specific language for this project and a supplemental section attached to further clarify the contract. Also, all the preliminary submissions are included as part of the overall contract. Specific to the contract is the construction limit of $38 million and a substantial completion date of July 2029. Background The proposed amendments update the City's Zoning Ordinance to maintain consistency with amendments to the Code of Virginia and ensure compliance with applicable state law. This round of text amendments relates to two new laws. • SB 531 added a section numbered § 15.2-2292.3 of the Code of Virginia, relating to zoning, development, and use of accessory dwelling units. • HB 655 amended and reenacted §§ 15.2-2247 and 15.2-2290 of the Code of Virginia, relating to zoning of manufactured housing. Overview The following sections of Chapter 286, Zoning, of the City Code are proposed to be amended pursuant to changes in the Code of Virginia related to SB 531 and HB 655: - §§ 286-202.04 Residential use types, 286-300.04 Permitted uses (RL Low Density Residential District), 286-302.04 Permitted uses (RM Medium Density Residential District), 286-304.04 Permitted uses (RH High Density Residential District), 286-308.04 Permitted uses (BB Boulevard Business District), 286-320.16 Definitions, 286-404.04 Accessory apartments, 286-404.24 Single-family, attached, 286-404.28 Single-family, detached, 286-404.16 Manufactured home, emergency, and 286-518.18 Minimum parking required. The amendments comply with the state requirements for manufactured housing by deleting the separate definitions for ‘Manufactured Home’ and ‘Manufactured Home, Emergency’ and including manufactured housing that meets certain standards as part of the definition for ‘SingleFamily Dwelling’. The use and design standards for ‘Manufactured Home, Emergency’ are converted to ‘Manufactured Home’ and establish general standards and emergency standards for PC Resolution 26-07/Ordinance 26-32 Page 2 of 2 manufactured housing whether used as a single-family dwelling or used temporarily as a result of an emergency situation. Staff Recommendation Staff recommends that the Planning Commission approve PC Resolution No. 26-07, recommending that the City Council adopt Ordinance No 26-32. ACCESSORY APARTMENT DWELLING UNIT A second dwelling unit within a detached single-family dwelling or within an accessory structure on the same lot as the detached single-family dwelling, which is clearly incidental and subordinate to the main dwelling unit. An attached or detached dwelling unit on a residential dwelling lot that provides complete independent living facilities for one or more individuals; is located on the same lot as a proposed or existing primary residence; and includes facilities for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation. *** MANUFACTURED HOME A single or multi-sectional manufactured home as defined in § 286-200 of this chapter. Manufactured housing that conforms to the real property requirements described in Section 286-404.16(A)(1), are deemed to be single-family, detached or single family detached. *** § 286-300 RL Low Density Residential District *** § 286-300.04 Permitted uses. *** (2) Residential use types: Accessory apartments dwelling units * Manufactured home, emergency* *** *** § 286-302 RM Medium Density Residential District *** § 286-302.04 Permitted uses. *** 2) Residential use types: Accessory apartments dwelling units * Manufactured home, emergency* *** *** § 286-304 RH High Density Residential District *** § 286-304.04 Permitted uses. ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 2 *** 2) Residential use types: Accessory apartments dwelling units * Manufactured home, emergency* *** *** § 286-306 RO Residential Office District *** § 286-306.04 Permitted uses. 2) Residential use types: *** Accessory apartments dwelling units* *** § 286-308 BB Boulevard Business District *** § 286-308.04 Permitted uses. 2) Residential use types: *** Single family dwellings, attached (S)* Single family dwellings, detached *** § 286-320.16 Definitions. A. Intent. Accessory apartments afford an opportunity for the development of small dwelling units designed to meet the housing needs of single persons, persons with fixed or limited income, and/or extended families who live or desire to live with a degree of privacy and independence. Accessory apartments provide a degree of flexibility for home owners with changing economic conditions and/or family structure, while providing a reasonable degree of protection for existing property values and neighborhood character. B. General standards. (1) Adequate parking, as determined by the Administrator, shall be provided. C. Additional standards in the RL, RM and RH Districts. (1) An accessory apartment shall only be considered as an accessory use to a detached single-family dwelling and no accessory apartment shall be located in any structure other than the principal structure on the lot, unless a special exception permit is approved for the accessory apartment. (2) Only one accessory apartment shall be allowed on any one lot or parcel, and the owner of the property shall reside on the premises, and only members of the owner's family shall reside in the accessory apartment. (3) No new exterior entrances to an accessory apartment within a detached single-family dwelling shall be allowed. Access to the accessory apartment must be through an existing exterior entrance. ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 4 (4) Upon completion of the construction, the accessory apartment shall not contain more than 50% of the finished floor area of the principal dwelling unit located on the same lot, but in no case shall the accessory apartment exceed 1,000 square feet. D. Additional standards in the RO District. (1) The accessory apartment shall be allowed only in the same structure as, and in conjunction with, an associated civic, office or commercial use type. (2) The civic, office or commercial use type must occupy at least 50% of the gross floor area of the structure. A. Accessory dwelling units, or “ADU”, as defined in Virginia Code § 15.2-2292.4, are authorized as a permitted accessory use for single family residential zoning districts. A permit must be obtained for the accessory dwelling unit. The permit shall be issued so long as the application conforms to the requirements described in § 15.2-2292.4, as well as the following requirements: (1) The primary dwelling's required parking must be replaced if the construction of the ADU eliminates such parking; (2) The ADU must have dedicated parking; (3) The footprint of any ADU shall not exceed 1,000 square feet or fifty (50) percent of the finished floor area of the principal dwelling unit located on the same lot, whichever is less; but in no case shall the maximum floor area be less than 350 square feet on lots less than 2,500 square feet or 500 square feet on lots 2,500 square feet or greater; (4) The ADU must be in compliance with (i) building codes, including the requirements of the Uniform Statewide Building Code (§ 36-97 et seq.), for an accessory dwelling unit if the ADU is attached or for a dwelling unit if the ADU is detached; (ii) water, sewer, septic, emergency access, ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 5 flood zone, and stormwater requirements; and (iii) historic and architectural districts and corridor protection restrictions; (5) Owner occupancy of the ADU or the primary dwelling, but not both, is required at the time an application is submitted to construct or convert an accessory dwelling unit; (6) The ADU shall be no more than 500 feet from the primary dwelling; (7) The ADU cannot be located on a residential lot that has more than one dwelling unit. B. In the event an ADU is leased, the rental term must be for 30 consecutive days or longer. Further, no ADU may be sold separately or otherwise subdivided from the primary dwelling. *** § 286-404.24 Single-family, attached. *** E. These regulations are adopted in recognition that temporary emergency housing options may be necessitated by fire, flood, or other unforeseen and sudden acts of nature. Call to Order: The City of Petersburg Planning Commission meeting held on Thursday, November 5, 2026, was called to order by Chair Ford at 6:00 p.m. 2. Roll Call: A quorum was established by Ms. Negasi. Vice-Chair Cannon arrived following the roll call. 3. Adoption of the Agenda: Chair Ford called for any proposed changes to the agenda. Commissioner Bland motioned to amend the agenda to delay the public hearing for 36 West Fillmore Street to next month’s meeting. Commissioner Bland stated he was informed by his attorney, Anthony Troy, that the hearing was not advertised within a 10-day requirement due to public hearing signs being posted 8 days prior to the meeting. Commissioner Hairston seconded the motion, which passed unanimously. Mr. Crews noted that Staff did meet advertisement requirements, explaining that the meeting was advertised in the local newspaper and written notices were mailed to adjoining property owners within the required timeframes. Mr. Crews noted that staff typically post signs on properties subject to special use permit requests, but this requirement is only mandatory for rezoning requests per the Zoning Ordinance. 3 The applicant stated the Commission motioned and voted before hearing if the legal requirements were met from Staff. The Commission discussed whether a previous vote could be revisited. Mr. Crews explained that Robert’s Rules of Order allows for a vote to be revisited during the same meeting on motion by a Commissioner who voted on the prevailing side of the original motion. Commissioner Katzenbach stated she was told by a member of the public that some individuals had left the hearing while the agenda was discussed. Commissioner Ford stated it is inappropriate for a member of the public to speak privately to a Commission member while the hearing is taking place. Commissioner Hairston stated he felt it would be an injustice to re-motion to keep the 36 West Fillmore Street hearing on the agenda while members of the public have left the audience. Commissioner Ford stated the applicant did not leave and was not given an explanation regarding the decision making. Commissioner Aku stated the Planning Commission is not responsible for whether members of the public leave during a hearing. Commissioner Ford stated the hearing will go to City Council, so members of the public will have an opportunity to be heard in front of Council. Commissioner Katzenbach stated the Planning Commission public hearing should take place before the applicant can present to City Council. Commissioner Katzenbach stated the public left after hearing the initial vote. Commissioner Aku stated the applicant is present and members of the public left on their own regard. Vice-Chair Cannon stated he has reconsidered his vote after hearing from Staff. He stated the public should not leave while a hearing is taking place. He also reiterated the public will have a chance to speak during the City Council hearing. Commissioner Hairston disagreed and reiterated his belief that proceeding with the hearing would be unfair to the public. Vice Chair Cannon motioned to revisit vote on agenda adoption. Commissioner Aku seconded, which passed 5-3, with Bland, Hairston, and Katzenbach opposing. Commissioner Norman motioned to adopt the agenda as originally drafted with the 36 Filmore Street hearing included. Vice-Chair Cannon seconded the motion, which passed 5-3, with Blan, Hairston, and Katzenbach opposing. 4 4. Consent Agenda: Commissioner Aku motioned to approve the consent agenda, which included minutes from the October 1st and 26th Planning Commission meetings. Vice-Chair Cannon seconded the motion, which passed 7-1-1, with Hariston abstaining. Commissioner Katzenbach asked when Staff would address concerns regarding the ordinance update that were discussed during the Special Planning Commission Meeting October 26th. Commissioner Ford responded stating the concerns would be addressed when the ordinance update is discussed on the agenda. 5. Public Comment: Chair Ford opened the floor for public comment. Hearing no comments, the public comment period was closed. 6. Public Hearings: a. 2026-SUP-06: Consideration of a resolution recommending approval of a request by Lawrence Ellis Williams Consulting LLC, on behalf of SP-Thirteen Properties LLC, for a special use permit to operate an assisted living facility at 36 West Fillmore Street, Parcel ID 022360001, in the RB Office-Apartment Zoning District (pages 18-88) Mr. Crews presented an overview of the Special Use Permit request for 36 Filmore Street, stating the applicant is seeking to operate an assisted living facility in an existing building on the property. Mr. Crews provided background information on the property, noting an assisted living facility operated there until 2022. Mr. Crews stated the current owner purchased the property in 2022 and completed renovations to re-establish assisted living facility use. Mr. Crews stated City Council adopted ordinance requiring a special use permit (SUP) for assisted living facilities in 2023 and the Board of Zoning Appeals overturned the Zoning Administrator’s determination that an assisted living facility was a legal nonconforming use of the property, meaning a special use permit was required. Mr. Crews stated a special use permit request had been submitted and subsequently denied on November 18, 2025. Mr. Crews stated the applicant is seeking to operate a 60-bed assisted living facility within the existing building on the site. Mr. Crews stated the facility would provide daily care and monitoring, medical oversight, medication and nutrition management, and supportive services for residents typically aged between 40-85 years of age. Mr. Crews stated the facility plans to provide 24-hour staffing and surveillance, including perimeter fencing and security cameras. Mr. Crews stated the application notes the facility does not intent to serve as a drug-treatment facility or a psychiatric treatment center. 5 Mr. Crews stated the applicant has offered voluntary conditions for consideration, in response to concerns raised during the public hearing for the prior request; 1. Facility will utilize screening process for residents to assess medical history, ability to function safely, physical and mental health support needs, behavioral history, and facility capabilities to meet needs 2. No more than 15% of residents will be between the age of 30 and 40 3. No more than 40 residents will be accepted during first year of operation 4. Facility will provide “Neighborhood Liaison” to be available to neighbors to address complaints or requests for management assistance 5. Facility will provide written rules of conduct as part of admission process; documented process will be used to address repeated violations possibly resulting in discharge 6. Facility will utilize resident sign-out and curfew requirements Mr. Crews stated staff has drafted a list of conditions for consideration: 1. Prior to the issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy (C/O) for the structure, the applicant shall address the active zoning violation on the property for replacement of the roof without the approval of the Architectural Review Board; the zoning violation shall be considered addressed when the asphalt shingle roof is replaced with a slate or synthetic slate roof in accordance with the April 12, 2023 ruling of the Architectural Review Board or otherwise if the Architectural Review Board votes to allow the existing roof to remain. 2. The site and facility shall be developed and maintained in substantial accordance with the Site Plans & Elevations and Floor Plans prepared by Lawrence Ellis Williams Consulting, LLC and dated August 15, 2025. 3. The facility shall obtain and maintain appropriate licensure through the Virginia Department of Social Services to operate as an assisted living facility in accordance with all provisions of Code of Virginia Section 63.2-1800, as amended; failure to maintain active licensure shall result in review and possible revocation of the special use permit. 4. In accordance with Code of Virginia, Section 63.-1805(d), as amended, the facility shall not admit or allow to remain any residents who present an imminent physical threat to themselves or others. 5. The facility shall be limited to a maximum of sixty (60) beds for residents, residency within the first year of operation shall not exceed forty (40) persons; any expansion beyond this number shall require an amendment to the approved special use permit. 6. No more than fifteen (15) percent of the resident population shall be between the ages of 30-39 at any one time; the remaining portion of the resident population shall be at least aged forty (40) or older. 6 7. The facility shall operate in accordance with all standards outlined in Virginia Administrative Code 22VAC-40-73, as amended, including, but not limited to the following: a. The facility shall have staff adequate in knowledge, skills, and abilities and sufficient in numbers to provide services to attain and maintain the physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident as determined by resident assessments and individualized service plans in accordance. b. The facility shall maintain a written plan that specifies the number and type of direct care staff required to meet the day-to-day, routine direct care needs and any identified special needs for the residents in care. This plan shall be directly related to actual resident acuity levels and individualized care needs. c. All staff who are mandated reporters under Section 63.2-1606 of the Code of Virginia, as amended, shall report suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of residents in accordance with that section. d. Resident sleeping quarters shall be provided and maintained in accordance with Virginia Administrative Code 22VAC40-73-900, as amended. 8. Qualified staff shall be on-site twenty-four (24) hours per day. Repeated substantiated complaints regarding adequate staffing and resident supervision shall result in review and possible revocation of the special use permit; the facility will provide and maintain a designated neighborhood liaison through which community members can communicate concerns with a dedicated telephone contact and email address made publicly available. 9. The special use permit serves as approval for use of the property as an assisted living facility as described in the Description of Facility Operations, Resident Population, Safety Measures, and Neighborhood Accountability narrative submitted by Stephen Parson, Executive Director/CEO of OneSource Community Mental Health Services of Virginia, Inc.; any expansion of the scope of services, including use of the facility as an outpatient clinic or medication assisted treatment facility is prohibited. 10. The development shall provide outdoor seating areas, including benches and tables, as well as at least two of the following outdoor resident amenities: gardening area(s), gazebo(s), outdoor fitness equipment, or gaming area. A plan identifying such amenities shall be provided to the Planning Department for review and approval prior to operation of the facility. 11. The on-site dumpsters shall be placed within an enclosed area consisting of opaque screening a minimum of six (6) feet in height. 12. Any new owner or operator of the facility must certify with the Zoning Administrator that the party will be undertaking the same or like endeavor and that their operation will remain in compliance with the approved special use permit. 7 13. This permit may be revoked by the City of Petersburg City Council or its designated agent for failure by the applicant to comply with any of the listed conditions or any provision of Federal, State, or local regulations. Mr. Crews stated the use being requested is substantively similar to the request that was reviewed and denied in 2025. Mr. Crews stated the use itself was what was reviewed and denied previously, but the applicant provided additional details with responses to the concerns that were identified during the initial request. Mr. Crews reminded the Commission the property is in active zoning violation for the roof. Mr. Crews stated the Architectural Review Board had given two years after their 2023 decision denying replacement of the roof, which expired in 2025. Mr. Crews noted to the Commission to consider whether the additional information and conditions provided are adequate to address the reasons the Commission recommended denial previously. Mr. Crews stated Commission has the option to approve with recommended, modified conditions, or the option to deny the application. Commissioner Ford asked the Commission if they have any questions for Staff. Commissioner Bland asked if the applicant has completed work on the roof. Mr. Crews confirmed the property’s roof is in active violation. Commissioner Katzenbach asked if there was any interaction with Architectural Review Board (ARB) requesting to stop repairs on the roof? Mr. Crews stated the roof repair was completed before the ARB reviewed the property. Mr. Crews stated the request was presented to the ARB retroactively, and ARB told the applicant to replace the roof with synthetic or true slate within a two-year timeframe. Commissioner Katzenbach stated she was told this was a criminal violation. Mr. Crews stated a criminal summons had been filed for the property, noting that all zoning violations are currently filed as criminal offenses. He asked that the applicant provide language to only allow seniors. 8 Mr. Crews stated the applicant can answer the question more directly, but the request was not specifically to open a senior living facility and the applicant had previously stated he would not be comfortable with any conditions limiting age to 60 years and above. Mr. Crews stated the facility would fall under the state’s definition of “assisted living facility” based on the licensing. Commissioner Hairston stated he is concerned that the facility may serve as a drug treatment facility. Mr. Crews stated the licensing for an assisted living facility is distinct from being licensed for a drug treatment facility. The applicant, Steve Parson, was present to speak in front of the Commission. Mr. Parson stated the management and operation of the former facility on the property was poor, noting the people he currently serves are outstanding individuals. Mr. Parson stated he passed inspection with Fire Marshal, Code Compliance, Zoning for the renovations of the facility and has done his part to guarantee the facility is safe and will present well in the community. Mr. Parson stated 15% percent of the 60 beds would be available for patients between 30-39 years old, and patients under the age of 30 would not be admitted. Commissioner Bland asked how long the roof repair would take if another extension were granted? Department of Planning & Community Development A meeting of the Franklin County Planning Commission was held on Tuesday, November 10, 2026 in the Board Room located at the Franklin County Government Center. THOSE PRESENT: Victor Evans – Chair, Union Hall District Ron Jefferson – Vice Chair, Gills Creek District David Pendleton – Blackwater District C.W. Doss – Blue Ridge District Addison Hancock – Snow Creek District Matthew Peters – Boone District OTHERS PRESENT: Lisa Cooper – Planning Director Jenn Richardson – Clerk Tina Franklin – Planner II Kathleen Duncan – Assistant Planning Director Chris Dadak – County Attorney THOSE ABSENT: NONE Chairman Evans called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. Mr. Evans asked if the Planning Commission had any comments or changes to the October 13, 2026 minutes. There were no changes requested. The minutes were approved as written. Mr. Evans introduced the next item on the agenda: APPLICATION for SPECIAL USE PERMIT – Application of Stanley Jones, Applicant, and Elemental Science Educational Support LLC, Owner, requesting a special use permit on an approximate 1.98 acres of property zoned A-1, Agricultural District. The parcel is located at 55 Woodman Road in the Union Hall Election District of Franklin County and further identified by real estate records as Tax Map/Parcel #0540007800. The purpose of this special use permit is to remove conditions two (2) (condition requiring adherence to VDOT regulations for the entrance) and Department of Planning & Community Development four (4) (condition requiring approvals and permitting from zoning, building, E&S control, and storm water management) and modify condition five (5) (condition requiring adherence to perimeter landscaping) from Resolution #07-07-2026 approved by the Board of Supervisors on July 21, 2026 for school (public and private). This property has a future land use designation of Low Density Residential - County (SPEC-26-10 #0510007800). Ms. Tina Franklin presented the staff report. She stated that in 1950 the existing building was constructed on the property identified as parcel id # 0540007800 and addressed as 55 Woodman Road and is +/- 1.960 acres. The property is zoned A1, Agricultural and has been used by the Woodmen of the World for many years as a community center and rented out for birthday parties and/or meetings. The Board of Supervisors approved a special use permit on July 21, 2026, for the purpose of a school (public and private) with the conceptual plan showing the location of a future building for a testing center. The property is served by a private well and septic system. The applicant stated in the letter of application that he would like to withdraw the proposed testing center from the application and as a result of this decision the conditions that were established in connection with that use are no longer applicable. The applicant indicated that with the proposed testing center removed from the application, the intended use of the property has changed. She stated that the applicant stated the revised proposed use could be for a community meeting space, community event space, and homeschool cooperative meeting which are consistent with the historical use of the property. The applicant requests that the Board review this matter and remove and/or amend the following conditions: • Remove condition #2. Compliance with all applicable VDOT entrance regulations. • Remove condition #4. Obtaining all required permits, including zoning, building, erosion and sediment control, and storm water management permits. • Amend condition #5 to state: “The applicant shall adhere to perimeter landscaping A between subject property and parcel id number 0540007400 (39 Woodman Road). Ms. Franklin stated that nearby parcels were single-family residential, farmland 2 Department of Planning & Community Development and vacant wooded lots with zoning of A-1, Agricultural, B-2, General Business and RC-1, Residential Combined Subdivision District. Woodman Road (State Route 706) is a state maintained secondary road. Ms. Franklin displayed four (4) GIS maps of the property and revised conceptual plan. Ms. Franklin stated the requested use was to amend the previously approved special use permit approved by the board of supervisors on July 21, 2026, referenced as a “school (public and private),” which is allowed by a special use permit approved by the Board of Supervisors. The requested amendment was to remove the new structure that was going to house a testing center and to remove condition two (2) requiring adherence to VDOT regulations for the entrance, remove condition four (4) requiring approvals and permitting from zoning, building, E&S control and storm water management, and to amend condition five (5) requiring adherence to perimeter landscaping and a minor site plan. With the new testing center structure removed from the project that was approved by the Board of Supervisors as a special use permit on July 21, 2026, county staff would not require a minor site plan and therefore there will be no plan for the county to require a review from VDOT on the entrance and traffic. The existing building will not require zoning and E&S control and storm water management review. Ms. Franklin stated there will be additional traffic that is generated from the new use (private educational facility); however, since this facility has been used for land use similarly in nature, staff does not anticipate problems with the road network or surrounding properties. The noise should be minimal with the proposed new use due to the fact testing and other educational functions will be indoors. Homeschoolers will benefit with hands-on laboratory education and other homeschool classes and activities. This facility would also continue to provide rental of the community center for birthday parties, meetings etc. for residents of the county. Ms. Franklin stated that staff recommended that the Planning Commission consider and approve the Special Use Permit amendment to allow for a school (public and private) with the following four (4) conditions: 1. The special use permit authorizing the use of an Elemental Science STEM Education Center on Tax Parcel # 0540007800 will be developed in substantial 3 Department of Planning & Community Development conformity with the concept plan entitled “Concept Plan: The Catalyst Station @ Woodman Road” dated September 2026 prepared by Stanley Jones. 2. The applicant must adhere to all VDH regulations regarding the septic system and well to ensure that it will support the proposed use. 3. If in the future the applicant/owner decides to expand the existing building or construct a new building, they will be required to amend the special use permit through the public hearing process. 4. The applicant shall adhere to perimeter landscaping A between subject property and parcel id number 0540007400 (39 Woodman Road). Ms. Franklin asked if the Planning Commission had any questions for her. Mr. Jefferson asked for clarification on the conditions. Ms. Franklin explained that Condition 5 was from the original Special Use Permit. The Planning Commission had no further questions for Ms. Franklin. Chairman Evans invited the applicant up to the podium to present. Mr. Stanley Jones presented a Powerpoint slideshow. Mr. Jones stated that he was the owner of Elemental Science Education Support. He stated that through his company, he had purchased the building. He stated that he had a new logo and that ‘Catalyst Station at Woodman Road’ would indicate the location, as well as reference science and the railroad heritage. Mr. Jones stated that he is interested in providing STEM education, homeschool co-ops, meetings and event space, and community learning. He stated that he was on his forty-first (41st) year of teaching. He stated that he is currently a chemistry instructor at Ferrum College. Mr. Jones stated that he retired from the state as an assistant professor of chemistry from the community college. He stated that he lives in Wade Park. Mr. Jones stated that from working with local parents and getting involved with homeschooling, it became apparent that there was a need for a more formal science education for homeschoolers. He stated that he has committed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) of his own investments for the project. He stated that he is using his own money to buy initial equipment to put into the building. Mr. Jones stated the he hopes to turn his LLC into a non-profit in order to use grants to purchase equipment and provide scholarships for students. He stated that he is currently doing a Mastering Chemistry course for homeschoolers. He stated that he is paid one 4 Department of Planning & Community Development hundred fifty dollars ($150) to teach the course, while Ferrum College is paid fifty dollars ($50) per credit hour to dual enroll in general chemistry I (1) and II (2). Mr. Jones stated that you can’t find anywhere in the country where you can get eight (8) credit hours of chemistry instruction for just five hundred dollars ($500). Mr. Jones stated that he hopes to create scholarship opportunities. Mr. Jones stated that he plans to hold workshops that will be open to all students. He stated that the current plan is to do a two (2) week workshop consisting of chemistry, physics, and a Mission To Mars, which would have problems that need to be solved that are similar to the Apollo 13 mission. He stated that he had one concern from a neighbor. He stated that he has agreed to put a boundary up to keep students off the neighboring property. Mr. Jones stated that he wanted an agricultural boundary. He stated that if the neighboring property decides that the kids are coming onto their property, they are more than welcome to put a fence up along the property line. Mr. Jones stated that his biggest hurdle was with VDOT. He stated that Woodman Road was a fifty-five (55) mph road because it doesn’t have a speed limit assigned. He stated that there was a ninety degree (90°) turn in the road. Mr. Jones stated that he was not asking to increase the use of the building other than what Woodman of the World had been doing since 1965. He stated that currently there is a two (2) hour sewing class on Mondays with sixteen (16) students and the Franklin County Citizens Commission meets in the building once a month. Mr. Jones stated that the VDOT requirement would make it economically impossible to do. He stated that to do a traffic study and other VDOT requirements would cost forty to sixty thousand dollars ($40,000-$60,000). Mr. Jones stated that there were nine (9) houses on Woodman Road and no recorded accidents for the past twenty (20) years. Mr. Jones stated that he is having community and meeting events at thirty-five dollars ($35) per hour to rent the building. He stated that the non-profit rate is twentyfive ($25) per hour. Mr. Jones stated that the local homeschool co-ops were paying a small fee to have access around the clock access to the building. He stated that it is going to be low impact to use fifteen (15) students at a time, there will not be a lot of traffic, and there is plenty of parking with a long, gravel driveway. Mr. Jones spoke about his background and his passion for teaching science. 5 Department of Planning & Community Development The Planning Commission had no questions for Mr. Jones. Mr. Evans opened the opportunity for citizen comment. There were no citizens who signed up to comment on the application. Seeing none and hearing none, the opportunity was closed. The Planning Commission began their deliberations. Mr. Jefferson asked for clarification on the VDOT requirements. Ms. Cooper stated that the conditions requested to be removed had to do with the new building that would serve as the testing center. She stated that it was going to be an expansion on the property and would require a minor site plan. She stated that they would also need to deal with erosion sediment controls, stormwater, and zoning and building permits. Ms. Cooper stated that a couple of months after the Board of Supervisors meeting, Mr. Jones contacted the Planning Department and asked if getting rid of the testing center would help with some of the VDOT requirements. Ms. Cooper stated that she met with Ms. Franklin and they determined it is an existing building, it was used as a community center. She stated that it was the chemistry and other classes that is requiring them to be school (public and private). Ms. Cooper stated that those VDOT conditions could be removed because the building was existing and most of the use there was existing. Mr. Jefferson clarified that VDOT’s original comments were tied to the minor site plan, and removing the minor site plan removed the requirement from VDOT. Ms. Cooper confirmed Mr. Jefferson’s statement. Mr. Jefferson made a motion stating “I find that such use will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property, that the character of the zoning district will not be changed thereby, and that such use will be in harmony with the purpose and intent of the County Code with the uses permitted by right in the zoning district, and with the public health, safety and general welfare to the community. Therefore, I move to recommend approval of the applicant’s request for a Special Use Permit amendment to remove conditions two (2) requiring adherence to VDOT regulations for the entrance, four (4) requiring approvals and permitting from zoning, building, E&S control and storm water management; and amend condition five (5) to remove submission of minor site plan in order to allow for a school (public and private) in accordance with Sec. 25-179 of the Zoning Ordinance, with the four (4) conditions as recommended in the staff report.” 6 Department of Planning & Community Development Mr. Hancock seconded the motion. text: MinutesoftheTownofBedford PLANNING COMMISSION The regular meeting of the Planning Commission was held on Thursday, November 5, 2026, in the Town Municipal Building Council Hall. Planning Commission members present: Jason Horne, Chairman; Darryl Updike, Town Council Representative; Cynthia Gunnoe; Georgiann Watts; and Philip Thompson Planning Commission member absent: Brock Malcolm, Vice Chair; and one vacancy Town Staff present: Mary Zirkle, Director of Planning and Community Development; and Cathy Johnson, Clerk of the Commission CALL TO ORDER: The Chair called the meeting to order at 5:30 pm. DETERMINATION OF QUORUM: There was a quorum to conduct business with five members present, one absent, and one vacancy. REMARKS BY CHAIRMAN & MEMBERS: Mr. Horne announced Mrs. Watts had resigned and it is her last meeting on the board. He took a moment to thank her for serving as a Commissioner. Mrs. Watts appreciated the acknowledgement and thanked the Board for the experience to serve. APPROVAL OF MINUTES: Mr. Updike made a motion to approve the minutes, which was seconded by Mrs. Watts. With five members voting aye, the October 1, 2026, minutes were approved as presented. STAFF AND COMMITTEE REPORTS: Ms. Zirkle thanked Mrs. Watts for her contribution on the board. She asked the Chair if she can give the updated process changes at the end of the meeting. He amended the agenda by stating that will be discussed at the end and he moved into discussion of New Business. NEW BUSINESS: Meyer Fingerer with Spring Oak Senior Living, located at 931 Ashland Avenue (formerly the Elks Home), presented a request for a sign modification to install three signs and he explained the primary purposes for the application were to improve emergency service access and to enhance marketing 11/5/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 1 of 6 visibility. He stated emergency services frequently enter the wrong driveway as the elevators and emergency entrance are located at the rear of the property. He stated prospective residents and approximately 60% of tourism from outside the local Bedford area reportedly have difficulty locating the facility. He stated that the existing signage is in poor condition and does not adequately identify the property. Mr. Horne asked is there anything in the zoning ordinance that addresses emergency access signage specifically. Staff indicated there is no specific provision for emergency access signs that would exempt them from permit requirements, though wayfinding signage may be an option worth exploring. Mr. Updike asked if the EMS entrance is the same entrance to the theater and Mr. Fingerer replied yes. Ms. Gunnoe asked will the existing sign posts be used and how much larger is the proposed sign compared to the existing one. Staff estimated the existing pole sign at approximately 30 square feet; the applicant indicated the existing sign including the logo is approximately 35 square feet, making the new reface sign only marginally larger and they will use the existing posts. Staff noted that the total signage area, when excluding the historic Elks National Home sign and the address, was approximately 63.3 square feet. The proposed total sign area still exceeds the 16-square-foot standard for non-residential uses in an R-1 zoning district, but less than the full 91.5 square feet listed in the application. Mr. Thompson asked how big was the property and is this a legal non-conforming use. The applicant stated the property spans approximately 29.87 acres. Staff stated because it operates as a nursing home in an R-1 zoning district, which is a legal non-conforming use. Since the request exceeded ordinance standards, it required Planning Commission action under the sign modification section. Mr. Thompson asked when will the signs be installed. The applicant indicated they would push for installation as quickly as possible, but it could take up to two months. Ms. Gunnoe made a motion to approve a sign modification for freestanding signs for Spring Oak as presented on the revised plans. Mr. Thompson seconded. The Chair asked for a roll-call and the votes were as followed: Mr. Updike Ms. Gunnoe Mr. Malcolm Mrs. Watts Mr. Thompson Mr. Horne Aye Aye Absent Aye Aye Aye The Planning Commission voted 5-0 to approve a sign modification for Spring Oak Bedford, LLC, at 931 Ashland Avenue to allow refacing an existing sign, two new signs on existing columns, and a new freestanding EMS sign on posts. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: The Commission reviewed updated draft language for the subdivision ordinance, focusing on pavement width standards and right-of-way dedication requirements. Ms. Zirkle read the pavement width text on page 19 to confirm wording. The revised pavement language confirmed that existing streets being continued shall have a minimum width of 30 feet exclusive of gutters, new streets shall have a minimum of 30 feet of pavement from face-to-face of curb, and streets with on-street parking shall require a minimum pavement width of 36 feet face-to-face of curb. Mr. Horne confirmed that the text was right. 11/5/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 2 of 6 A discussion arose regarding the treatment of "future" or "proposed" right-of-way on plats. Ms. Gunnoe expressed concern that applicants were submitting plats showing right-of-way that had not yet been formally dedicated, which could lead to landlocked parcels or unresolved access issues. She asked should the ordinance include language requiring proof of right-of-way access before a subdivision application is reviewed. Staff stated the subdivision ordinance already requires all right-of-way to be shown on the plat for dedication. Mr. Thompson agreed that only formally dedicated right-of-way should be shown on plats. The consensus was that a right-of-way is only valid when formally dedicated through plat recordation, and that "future" right-of-way designations should not be accepted as meeting access requirements. Additional discussion covered restrictive covenants, homeowner associations, and the Town's limited ability to enforce private covenants. Ms. Gunnoe asked can the Town require applicants to show how restrictive covenants will be enforced. Staff stated that covenant enforcement is a private civil matter between property owners or homeowner associations and the courts. The Town does not have jurisdiction unless the covenant is tied to a condition or proffer from a land use approval. The ordinance does require that any restrictive covenants be referenced on the plat so buyers are aware of them. The Commission also reviewed the timeline changes related to state-mandated review periods, noting that the review window has been reduced from 60 days to 45 days per new state code requirements. The Commission wanted to know if the pre-application meeting is optional or mandatory. Staff confirmed that state code prohibits making the pre-application meeting mandatory; it must remain optional. Next, item of unfinished business, Ms. Zirkle presented proposed amendments to the floodplain ordinance, which is structured as a Flood Hazard Overlay District within the zoning ordinance. The amendments are intended to bring the Town into compliance with the current Virginia state model ordinance, as required by the Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR). The changes are primarily definitional and do not represent a substantive overhaul of the existing regulations, which already closely track the state model. The Town is currently operating under 2010 FEMA floodplain maps. New preliminary maps have been released, and approximately 300 to 350 parcels show some change in floodplain designation. However, the 90-day public appeal process with FEMA has not yet begun. Once the new maps are finalized with the anticipated time around 2028, the Town will need to hold an additional public hearing to update the effective map date in the ordinance. Mr. Thompson asked when the new FEMA maps are adopted and the ordinance date is updated, will affected property owners need to be individually notified. Ms. Zirkle indicated that property owners are being notified through the current FEMA appeal process. She stated when the Town later amends the ordinance to update the map date, it is treated similarly to a zoning overlay change affecting more than 25 properties, which under State code does not necessarily require individual property owner notification and she would confirm this with DCR. Mr. Thompson asked why was the floodplain ordinance kept within the zoning ordinance rather than made a standalone document. Staff explained that separating it would have required users to cross-reference two documents to determine floodplain status while keeping it as an overlay within the zoning ordinance was more practical for zoning review. Mr. Thompson asked should the Town adopt the FEMA-recommended 18-inch freeboard standard for construction above base flood elevation, rather than the current 12-inch minimum required by state code. Ms. Zirkle stated DCR indicated 18 inches is becoming more common nationally and may eventually be 11/5/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 3 of 6 required, but adopting 12 inches now could require another amendment in the near future. The Commission acknowledged the risk of having to amend the ordinance again soon if 12 inches is adopted now, and they agreed to discuss this further during the public hearing. At the last meeting, the Commissioners suggested combining public hearings for the subdivision and floodplain ordinance amendments into a single advertised hearing with two separate actions tentatively scheduled for the December meeting. Mr. Thompson made a motion to combine the subdivision ordinance and floodplain ordinance amendments into a single advertised public hearing on December 3. Ms. Gunnoe seconded. The Chair asked for a roll-call and the votes were as followed: Mr. Updike Ms. Gunnoe Mr. Malcolm Mrs. Watts Mr. Thompson Mr. Horne Aye Aye Absent Aye Aye Aye The Planning Commission voted 5-0 to combine the subdivision ordinance and floodplain ordinance amendments for a single advertised public hearing on December 3, 2026. STAFF AND COMMITTEE REPORTS - continuation: Ms. Zirkle provided an update on the status of towing operations within the Town, following earlier requests from operators seeking to establish towing offices. She stated the State Police have divided the Town into zones, and towing operators must be located within a zone to be dispatched for calls in that area. This has prompted multiple operators to seek office locations in Town. After a visit from the Virginia State Police officer for the program, she clarified that a towing office, as defined by the State Police, requires an exterior or interior impound lot along with proper signage, a fenced and locked storage area or secure garage, on-site recordkeeping, and storage of all vehicles at the approved location. She stated this definition is incompatible with the Town's current zoning, which does not permit automotive impound uses as an accessory use. The State Police have indicated they will remove noncompliant operators from their dispatch list unless the Town provides a letter of approval confirming that each address is permitted for towing operations. She is working through this process and can only issue letters for the two legally operating locations - Fat Boys on Industrial Avenue and Big Toe, which was associated with Rowlett’s Auto & Tire on Plunkett Street. When asked by the Commissioners, what was the status of the operator who previously appeared before them, Ms. Zirkle stated that the operator proceeded his operation anyway without approval. The Commissioners asked staff how does the County handle towing operations. Ms. Zirkle replied that the County similarly allows a towing office but requires a conditional use permit for the impound component of the operation. Next, as discussed at the last meeting, Ms. Zirkle provided a drafted AI-policy for project review for Commission action. She also asked them to review site plan items required in Section 1002 of the zoning ordinance since Commissioners informed staff they were not getting enough information before hearings. 11/5/26 Planning Commission Minutes - Page 4 of 6 Ms. Zirkle stated in addition to the combined subdivision and floodplain ordinance public hearing, there are three possible land use public hearings for the next meeting, and she provided applications for two the Town received. She summarized the following: (1) Property on Ruff Drive was previously denied a variance by the Board of Zoning Appeals is exercising its option to rezone from M-1, Manufacturing District to R-1, Single-Family Residential District, in order to allow residential use to continue and expand. (2) The Harmony Crossing developer has requested to convert a previously approved commercial area within a Planned Development District to 162 apartment units. Staff stated this cannot be approved administratively and requires a formal zoning amendment. Mr. Thompson asked will the Harmony Crossing developer submit renderings and a traffic study with their application. Ms. Zirkle stated a traffic impact study completed by Westwood Professional Services indicates lower traffic generation compared to the previously approved commercial use. She will request that the developer submit renderings prior to the next meeting and she will confirm the traffic study has been submitted to VDOT. (3) A recently zoned property located on Forest Road, as part of the second phase boundary adjustment, is expected to submit a request to expand permitted uses beyond what is allowed under LP, Limited Professional zoning district to CLI, Commercial Light Industrial district. Lastly, she stated that Town Council will appoint two new Planning Commission members at their next meeting to fill the two vacancies. She concluded that training for new members is planned for early next year.
